planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, and again every 10-14 days for a continuous harvest through cool weather.

directions: Cherriette is an F1 hybrid improvement on the classic Cherry Belle type, bred for extra uniformity and unusual resistance to pithiness even if roots are left in the ground past ideal size. Sow seed shallowly in loose, stone-free soil and thin early so roots have room to size up into smooth, bright cherry-red globes with dense, crisp white flesh. Its speed and evenness make it a favorite for market growers who need a reliable, uniform crop, while home gardeners appreciate that a missed harvest window rarely ruins the eating quality.

planting.note: Sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest, since roots develop their best flavor and store best when they mature in cool weather.

directions: Nero Tondo, Italian for round black, is a refined selection of the old Black Spanish type bred for rounder, more uniform roots and notably better bolt tolerance than the traditional heirloom strain. The rough, matte-black skin conceals dense, snow-white flesh with a sharp, peppery bite that mellows into an earthy sweetness when roasted or braised. Because the roots hold in the ground and in storage far longer than spring radishes, gardeners grow it as a keeper crop, pulling roots through fall and into winter for slaws, pickles, and cooked preparations.

planting.note: Sow from late spring through midsummer since Mino Early tolerates heat and resists bolting better than most daikon types, making it a reliable choice for a summer-to-fall crop.

directions: Mino Early is an old open-pollinated Japanese heirloom prized for producing long, slender white roots weeks faster than standard Minowase types, with late-developing pithiness that keeps texture crisp even at full size. Work soil deeply and stone-free before sowing, since the smooth cylindrical roots can reach 14-16 inches and require loose ground to grow straight. Its combination of speed, heat tolerance, and mild, tender flavor makes it a dependable choice for growers wanting daikon without the long season standard winter types demand.

scientific_name: Raphanus sativus var. longipinnatus 'Summer Cross No. 3'

planting.note: Sow from late spring into midsummer; this hybrid was specifically bred to resist bolting and disease under the heat and humidity that cause most daikon to fail in summer plantings.

directions: Bred by Takii as a Minowase-type hybrid for the summer sowing window, Summer Cross No. 3 combines a distinctive white-shouldered, cylindrical root with strong tolerance to heat, virus, and Fusarium wilt that ordinarily plague daikon planted before cool fall weather sets in. Direct sow into deeply worked soil and thin to a wide final spacing so roots can size up straight and unforked. Growers who want daikon in mid-to-late summer, rather than waiting for a fall-only crop, choose this hybrid specifically for its ability to hold quality and resist bolting through hot conditions that would ruin open-pollinated types.

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring for a summer crop, or sow again in mid-to-late summer for a fall harvest, since roots develop their sweetest flavor in cool weather.

directions: Named for Croissy-sur-Seine, a historic market-gardening town near Paris, this French heirloom produces slightly curved, cylindrical white roots that were traditionally bunched and sold young for their tender, sweet flesh. It matures faster than globe-type turnips, making it well suited to close spring and late-summer sowings where a quick, mild crop is wanted before or after the main season. Its half-long, tapered shape and old-market-garden history distinguish it from the round purple-top types that dominate most American gardens.

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring or late summer; Savanna tolerates more heat than most mustard without bolting, extending the harvest window on both ends of the season.

directions: Savanna is a fast-growing F1 hybrid mustard bred for exceptionally tender, smooth leaves and stems that stay mild and non-fibrous even as plants size up, letting the whole leaf and stem be harvested without trimming. It grows quickly enough to cut for baby salad greens within three weeks or left longer for a traditional cooked green, and its slow-bolting habit keeps it productive across a wider temperature range than older open-pollinated Southern mustards. Home gardeners and market growers choose it for cut-and-come-again harvesting, since new leaves regrow readily after cutting through the cool season.
